tagline.text: A national cultural treasure museum preserving the records of the world's largest leprosy colony

location.label: Location
location.text: Inside the Culion Sanitarium and General Hospital compound, Barangay Tiza, Culion, Palawan

children.text: Located inside the hospital compound on Culion Island, south of Coron, this museum displays photos, currency, research tools and documents from the leprosy colony founded in 1906. It was added to the UNESCO Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Register in 2018 and declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2024.

The Culion Museum and Archives is a small museum inside the Culion Sanitarium and General Hospital compound in Barangay Tiza, on Culion Island in the Calamian group of northern Palawan. The building is the former laboratory used for leprosy research, built by the Leonard Wood Memorial in
, and it opened as a museum in 1997. It still sits within the hospital grounds, so it feels less like a tourist attraction and more like stepping into a corner of a working medical facility.

Culion became a leprosy segregation colony on May 27, 1906, when two government coast guard cutters brought 370 patients from Cebu and landed them on the island. New patients from all over the Philippines arrived about every three months, and by 1910 around 5,300 people had been sent there, making it known as the largest leprosy colony in the world at the time. Records say more than 3,000 of them died of the disease and the harsh conditions. From the 1920s, research funding grew and Culion became a research hub that drew leprologists from around the world, while residents elected their own representatives and used their own currency in a town built around the colony.

The museum tells the story from the founding of the colony in 1906 to the development of multi-drug therapy (MDT) in the 1980s. On the ground floor you learn about the island's history, the daily life of patients and an explanation of the disease, and on the upper floor you find a memorial honoring the doctors, nurses, pharmacists, priests, pastors and technicians who cared for the patients. The collection of documents, photos and letters goes back to 1906, and on May 30, 2018 the Culion leprosy archives were inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World Asia and the Pacific Regional Register. In 2024 the museum was also declared a National Cultural Treasure of the Philippines.

For travelers, it is the most meaningful history stop you can reach as a day trip from Coron. However, opening hours are short and limited to weekdays, and because it is inside a hospital you need to visit quietly, so planning your schedule around it matters. The information below is based on 2013 and 2018 visitor accounts and official sources, so check fares and ferry schedules before you go.

The ground floor has a room about Culion's first days as a leprosy colony, a patient's bed, a detailed explanation of the disease and before-and-after photos of treated patients. A replica of the nursery, where babies were separated from their parents and could be seen only through a glass window, along with a photo of the real nursery, is often named as the most memorable display.

Inside the colony, a separate currency used only on the island was issued so that money handled by patients would not leave it. You can see the actual currency in a ground-floor display case, and the coins and notes show how strictly the segregation policy was enforced at the time.

A map from the 1920s shows the town divided into a patient side and a staff side. The gates that separated the two areas still stand around town, so after seeing the museum you can look for them and watch the lines on the map turn into real scenery.

Because the building itself was a leprosy research laboratory, the museum has equipment used by doctors and scientists, research tools and a patient's sickbed. On the upper floor you will also find a photo of Dr. Jose Rodriguez, a pioneer in leprosy research.

The upper floor honors the doctors, nurses, pharmacists, priests, pastors and technicians who cared for patients. The exhibit covers not only the patients' suffering but also the dedication of those who worked beside them, helping visitors read Culion's story without taking only one side.

blocks.title: Memory of the World and national treasure

children.text: The collection, inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World Asia-Pacific Register in 2018 and declared a National Cultural Treasure in 2024, is organized into about 30 series. Hospital staff describe these records as the story of people who lived with dignity despite incredible hardship.

Nearby, La Inmaculada Concepcion Church was built in the 17th century by the Augustinian Recollects on a coral-based foundation, and the neighboring Fort Culion, built around 1740, still has its cannons and views over the sea and the town.

A climb of more than 330 steps brings you to a viewpoint with a monument resembling Christ the Redeemer in Rio. The climb is fairly steep, but the town and the sea spread out below you. Be sure to bring water.

items.title: Day trip from Coron
items.subtitle: The museum and a loop around town

children.text: Head from central Coron to the pier for the fast craft to Culion. In 2018 the first boat left at
, so check the schedule the day before.
Arrive at Culion port and take a tricycle to the hospital gate. The museum is inside the hospital compound, so tell the staff at the gate you are going to the museum and follow their directions.
Start on the ground floor in the morning. Allow about an hour for Culion’s early history, the nursery reconstruction, patient beds, local currency and the town map.
Go upstairs to see the research tools, the memorial and the photo of Dr. Rodriguez. A hospital staff member or caretaker often adds a little commentary.
Return to town for lunch at a place such as the Hotel Maya restaurant. Visitors have reported rice meals at around
In the afternoon, see the remaining exhibits or walk to the church, fort and old gate between the patient and staff areas.
If you still have energy, climb the steps to Agila Viewpoint, then return to the port before sunset. As of 2018 the last boat back to Coron left at

The museum is open on weekdays, Monday to Friday, and is closed on weekends and holidays. The schedule above comes from 2018, so check the latest boat times at the Coron pier or your accommodation before planning.

items.title: 2 days, 1 night
items.subtitle: The museum and a viewpoint hill

children.text: Check the boat departure from Coron and visit both floors of the museum in the morning.
Drop your bags at a place like Hotel Maya, then see the church, the fort and Agila Viewpoint.
Eat dinner at a restaurant near the port and watch the sunset from a viewpoint hill above town.
Rent a motorbike and watch the sunrise from Pulang Lupa hill. Reports say the hike takes 1–2 hours on foot or 20–30 minutes by motorbike.
If you have time, snorkel at the Crowning Glory Reef marine protected area, then take the boat back to Coron.
Some parts of Culion have unreliable electricity late at night, so bring a power bank.
Culion has no airport, so fly from Manila to Busuanga (Coron) Airport, USU, and continue by road and boat.
Flight times from Manila to Busuanga differ by airline, so check when you book. The flight usually takes around one hour.

Staying near central Coron or the pier makes it easier to catch the first boat in the morning.

The easiest way to get from the port to the hospital with the museum is by tricycle.
The town is walkable, and a local tour operator in Culion has been reported renting motorbikes for about
a day.
Enter the museum with guidance from the hospital gate, and walk quietly because it is a hospital compound.

The museum is indoors, so weather matters little, but the sea crossing from Coron to Culion is affected by conditions. The dry season from November to May usually brings calmer seas and is also good for the viewpoint and hill routes.
The museum itself was damaged by Typhoon Haiyan (Yolanda) in 2013, reopened on July 26, 2014, and reopened again in November 2019. It is safest to check whether it is open before you visit.

The
Culion Sanitarium and General Hospital visitor guide
lists the Museum & Archives as open Monday to Friday,
, excluding holidays. Arrange weekend and holiday visits with the hospital in advance.
Withdraw plenty of cash in Coron. Many places in Culion do not accept cards or traveler's checks, and small bills are handy.
Visitors have reported that Globe 4G worked well. Wi-Fi is limited, so download maps in advance.
The museum is inside the hospital compound, so tell the gate staff you are going to the museum, and ask the front desk about the admission fee.
Agila Viewpoint has many steps, so climb in the morning or after the sun has dropped, and bring water and a hat.
A day trip is tight because of the boat times, so if the museum is your goal, focus on the museum and the church and fort, and save snorkeling for an overnight stay.
There are few places to book other than Hotel Maya, so contact them from Coron in advance or get help from a local tour operator.
It helps to bring insect repellent, reef-safe sunscreen and a reusable water bottle.
The museum opens only on weekdays and its hours are short because of collection care. Check the latest opening schedule and boat times first.
This is a hospital and care facility compound, and people still live here. When taking photos, avoid capturing people's faces, and visit quietly.
Fares, ferry schedules and opening hours mix 2013–2018 sources and may have changed. Confirm on site.
Some outlying areas of Culion have unreliable electricity and mobile coverage. Bring a power bank for remote itineraries.
There are only a few boats a day and they may be canceled in bad weather, so stick to the last boat time. On a day trip, do not miss the boat back.
Leprosy has long been a target of prejudice. Do not treat the exhibits as pity or spectacle, and approach them as history with respect.
This is the whole island that holds the museum. It has a church and fort, Agila Viewpoint, the Pulang Lupa hill and Crowning Glory Reef, so it pairs well with a museum visit.
The port town where boats to Culion depart. It is a hub for island hopping and diving off Coron, and a good place to stay before or after a museum trip.
